idiom_name: subject with a subscription registry + notification loop
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the subject a registry of observers (list, set or per-event map), an attach/detach operation that returns a removal handle, and a notify step that runs after the state is consistent and iterates over a snapshot of the registry. Depend on the abstract update operation instead of concrete observers, and pass the change with the notification (event object, old and new value, or the subject itself) so observers do not have to poll. Decide and document three contracts up front: who owns the observer's lifetime (strong reference plus explicit detach, or weak reference), which thread notifies and whether subscribe/notify may be concurrent, and what happens when a handler throws or detaches during the notification loop. In Python the callable form eliminates the interface entirely; in TypeScript prefer typed event interfaces over string event names to catch typos at compile time. For async fan-out, await all observers concurrently with asyncio.gather() or equivalent; use gather(return_exceptions=True) for fire-and-continue semantics, or a task group only when you want one failure to cancel the rest.
code_sketch:
subject.subscribe(observer) -> handle      # returns a removal handle / disposable
subject.unsubscribe(handle)
on state change:
    snapshot = copy(registry)             # handlers may detach while we iterate
    for observer in snapshot:
        observer.update(event)            # never under the subject's lock
pitfalls: Notifying from inside a mutation while the state is still inconsistent: observers that read back see a half-updated subject.
No removal handle or weak reference for subscribers the subject does not own, so dead observers are kept alive and keep being notified.
Running handlers while holding the subject's lock, which deadlocks the first time a handler subscribes or notifies.
Iterating the registry directly while handlers detach (e.g., one-shot self-removing observer) — the loop index shifts and skips the next entry.
Discarding the coroutine from an async setter: assigning the result of an async def drops the coroutine; the state change never runs.

Using AbortSignal as a substitute for explicit unsubscribe: AbortSignal makes cleanup convenient but trades deterministic cleanup for non-deterministic GC timing — a strong reference held elsewhere still prevents collection.

Wrong move: let observers coordinate through hidden shared mutable state and side effects -> reactions become hard to compose, can violate encapsulation, and make lifecycle/disposal ownership unclear -> instead pass typed event data, keep reactions independent, and choose an explicit reactive/dataflow abstraction when transformations must compose.
